celestialTypes.Name: inferred from gravitational effects and cosmic expansion

instruments.Description: A wide-field survey telescope that will provide deep images of the sky in multiple wavelengths.
instruments.Name: Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST)

instruments.Description: A space-based observatory that measured the cosmic microwave background radiation across the entire sky.
instruments.Name: Planck Satellite

instruments.Description: A space-based observatory designed to detect X-ray emissions from very hot regions of the universe.
instruments.Name: Chandra X-ray Observatory

instruments.Description: Two large optical telescopes located in Hawaii, known for their large apertures and adaptive optics.
instruments.Name: Keck Observatory

instruments.Description: An array of radio telescopes located in the Atacama Desert of Chile, used for observing millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths.
instruments.Name: Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA)

instruments.Description: A large, space-based observatory designed to observe the universe in the infrared spectrum.
instruments.Name: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)

instruments.Description: A space-based observatory that has provided high-resolution images and data of space objects.
instruments.Name: Hubble Space Telescope (HST)

instruments.Description: An array of four optical telescopes located in Chile, operated by the European Southern Observatory.
instruments.Name: Very Large Telescope (VLT)

theories.Summary: This theoretical framework aims to reconcile general relativity (describing gravity) with quantum mechanics, potentially leading to a unified description of all forces at very high energies or small scales.
theories.Name: Quantum Gravity

theories.Summary: Scientists have proposed theories to unify these forces. The electroweak theory successfully unifies the electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces. Efforts to unify all four forces, such as Grand Unified Theories (GUTs) and string theory, are still under development.
theories.Name: Unification Theories

forces.Relative Strength: Stronger than gravity but weaker than both the electromagnetic and strong nuclear forces
forces.Range: Extremely short range (less than a femtometer)
forces.Description: This force is responsible for processes like beta decay in radioactive atoms. It affects all fermions (quarks and leptons) and plays a crucial role in nuclear reactions, such as those that fuel the sun.
This force binds protons and neutrons together in an atomic nucleus. It is the strongest force but acts only over very short distances, typically on the order of a femtometer (10^-15 meters).

forces.Relative Strength: Stronger than gravity but weaker than the strong nuclear force
forces.Description: This force acts between electrically charged particles. It governs phenomena like electricity, magnetism, and light, and it plays a crucial role in the structure of atoms and molecules.

This force attracts two bodies with mass toward each other. It is responsible for the structure and dynamics of the cosmos on a large scale, such as the orbits of planets, the formation of stars, and the behavior of galaxies.

spectralTypes.Characteristics: Extremely cool, with ammonia features in their spectra.
spectralTypes.Name: Y-type Stars (Y Dwarfs)

spectralTypes.Characteristics: Very cool, with strong methane absorption bands.
spectralTypes.Name: T-type Stars (T Dwarfs)

spectralTypes.Characteristics: Cool, with metal hydride and alkali metal lines, dusty atmospheres.
spectralTypes.Name: L-type Stars (L Dwarfs)

spectralTypes.Characteristics: Strong molecular bands, especially titanium oxide.
spectralTypes.Name: M-type Stars

spectralTypes.Characteristics: Weak hydrogen lines, strong metal lines, and molecular bands.
spectralTypes.Name: K-type Stars

spectralTypes.Characteristics: Weak hydrogen lines, strong ionized calcium lines. Our Sun is a G-type star.
spectralTypes.Name: G-type Stars

spectralTypes.Characteristics: Moderate hydrogen lines, stronger metal lines than A-type.
spectralTypes.Name: F-type Stars

spectralTypes.Characteristics: Hot, with prominent hydrogen lines and neutral helium lines.
spectralTypes.Name: B-type Stars

spectralTypes.Characteristics: Strong hydrogen lines, some metal lines.
spectralTypes.Name: A-type Stars

spectralTypes.Characteristics: Very hot and massive, with strong ionized helium lines and weak hydrogen lines.
spectralTypes.Name: O-type Stars

rockTypes.Comment: formed from layers of sand, silt, dead plants, and animal skeletons.
rockTypes.Name: Sedimentary rocks

rockTypes.Comment: formed from other rocks that are changed by heat and pressure underground.
rockTypes.Name: Metamorphic rocks

rockTypes.Comment: formed from melted rock deep inside the Earth.
rockTypes.Name: Igneous rocks

equations.Symbols: γ the stretch factor · v relative speed · c speed of light · equals 1 at rest, grows without bound as v approaches c
equations.Significance: The exchange rate of relativity: moving clocks run slow by γ, moving rulers shrink by γ, and kinetic energy diverges as v nears c — which is why nothing with mass reaches light speed. At everyday speeds γ is 1 to a dozen decimal places, which is why none of this is felt.
equations.Name: Lorentz Factor

equations.Equation: x′ = γ(x − vt) · t′ = γ(t − vx/c²)
equations.Symbols: x, t position and time in one frame · x′, t′ the same event seen from a frame moving at speed v · c speed of light · γ the Lorentz factor · y and z pass through unchanged
equations.Significance: How space and time coordinates convert between observers in relative motion — and the surprise is that time mixes with position. Written by Lorentz to patch electromagnetism; reinterpreted by Einstein in 1905 as the actual geometry of space and time. Simultaneity has been relative ever since.
equations.Name: Lorentz Transformations

equations.Symbols: S entropy of a perfect crystal · T absolute temperature
equations.Significance: As temperature approaches absolute zero, entropy approaches a constant floor — zero for a perfect crystal. Consequence: absolute zero itself can be approached but never reached, no matter how clever the refrigerator.
equations.Name: Third Law of Thermodynamics

equations.Symbols: ΔS change in total entropy of an isolated system · equality only for reversible processes
equations.Significance: Disorder never decreases on its own: heat flows hot to cold, engines can't be perfect, and time gets its arrow. Born from Carnot's steam-engine analysis, named by Clausius — arguably the most unbreakable law in physics.
equations.Name: Second Law of Thermodynamics

equations.Named After: Julius Robert von Mayer · James Joule · Rudolf Clausius
equations.Symbols: ΔU change in internal energy · Q heat added to the system · W work done by the system
equations.Significance: Energy is never created or destroyed, only moved and converted — heat in, work out, the books always balance. The law that retired the perpetual-motion machine.
equations.Name: First Law of Thermodynamics

equations.Equation: T₁ = T₃ and T₂ = T₃ ⟹ T₁ = T₂
equations.Symbols: T₁, T₂, T₃ temperatures of three systems · systems in thermal equilibrium share a temperature
equations.Significance: If two systems each sit in equilibrium with a third, they're in equilibrium with each other — the quiet assumption that makes 'temperature' a well-defined number and thermometers meaningful. So foundational it was named zeroth, after the first and second were taken.
equations.Name: Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics

equations.Symbols: Δx uncertainty in position · Δp uncertainty in momentum · ℏ reduced Planck constant
equations.Significance: Position and momentum cannot both be pinned down — sharpen one and the other blurs. Not a limit of instruments but of nature itself: it keeps electrons from collapsing into nuclei and gives atoms their size.
equations.Name: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle

equations.Symbols: λ wavelength associated with a particle · h Planck constant · p momentum
equations.Significance: If light can act like particles, matter can act like waves — every moving thing has a wavelength. Electrons diffract like light does, which is why electron microscopes see atoms and why atoms have discrete orbitals at all.
equations.Name: De Broglie Wavelength

equations.Symbols: B magnetic field · J current density · E electric field · μ₀ permeability of free space · ε₀ permittivity of free space · t time
equations.Significance: Currents make magnetic fields — and, Maxwell's crucial addition, so do changing electric fields. That extra term closes the loop: E and B can regenerate each other and race through empty space as light, at exactly c. Fourth of Maxwell's equations, completing the set with Gauss's two laws and Faraday's.
equations.Name: Ampère–Maxwell Law

equations.Symbols: E electric field · B magnetic field · ∇× curl (circulation around a point) · t time
equations.Significance: A changing magnetic field stirs up a circulating electric field — the principle inside every generator, transformer, and induction cooktop. Third of Maxwell's four equations.
equations.Name: Faraday's Law of Induction

equations.Symbols: B magnetic field · ∇· divergence (net outflow from a point)
equations.Significance: Magnetic field lines never start or end — there are no magnetic monopoles. Cut a magnet in half and you get two magnets, never a lone north pole. Second of Maxwell's four equations.
equations.Name: Gauss's Law for Magnetism

equations.Symbols: T orbital period · a semi-major axis of the orbit · G gravitational constant · M mass of the central body
equations.Significance: Orbital period squared scales with orbit size cubed — the harmony that let Newton reverse-engineer the inverse-square law, and how we weigh stars, planets, and black holes today.
equations.Name: Kepler's Third Law

equations.Symbols: A area swept by the Sun–planet line · t time · L orbital angular momentum · m planet mass
equations.Significance: The line to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times: planets hurry through closest approach and dawdle far away. Conservation of angular momentum, decades before the concept had a name.
equations.Name: Kepler's Second Law

equations.Symbols: r distance from the Sun · p semi-latus rectum (size of the orbit) · e eccentricity (0 circle, <1 ellipse) · θ angle from closest approach
equations.Significance: Planets travel ellipses with the Sun at one focus — not the perfect circles two millennia of astronomy insisted on. Written as the polar equation of the orbit.
equations.Name: Kepler's First Law

equations.Symbols: p pressure · V volume · n moles · R gas constant · T absolute temperature · a attraction between molecules · b volume the molecules themselves occupy
equations.Significance: The ideal gas law with reality patched in: molecules attract each other and take up space. Explains why real gases condense into liquids — which pV = nRT never could.
equations.Name: Van der Waals Equation

equations.Symbols: r rate of effusion through a small opening · M molar mass · subscripts: the two gases compared
equations.Significance: Light molecules escape faster, in inverse proportion to the square root of their mass — why helium balloons deflate overnight, and the principle behind uranium enrichment by diffusion.
equations.Name: Graham's Law of Effusion

equations.Symbols: p total pressure of the mixture · p₁, p₂, … partial pressure each gas would exert alone
equations.Significance: Gases in a mixture ignore each other: each contributes its own pressure independently. How divers compute oxygen dose and how the atmosphere's 21% oxygen is meant.
equations.Name: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures

equations.Symbols: V volume · n amount of gas (moles) · subscripts: two samples · holds at constant temperature and pressure
equations.Significance: Equal volumes of any gas hold equal numbers of molecules — the insight that made molecular formulas countable and gave the mole its meaning.
equations.Name: Avogadro's Law

equations.Symbols: p pressure · T absolute temperature · subscripts: two states · holds at constant volume and amount
equations.Significance: In a rigid container, pressure tracks absolute temperature — why a sealed can builds pressure in a fire, and why tire pressure reads higher after the drive.
equations.Name: Gay-Lussac's Law

equations.Symbols: V volume · T absolute temperature · subscripts: two states · holds at constant pressure and amount
equations.Significance: Warm a gas and it swells in proportion to absolute temperature — hot-air balloons in one line, and an early signpost pointing at absolute zero.
equations.Name: Charles's Law

equations.Symbols: p pressure · V volume · subscripts: two states of the same gas · holds at constant temperature and amount
equations.Significance: Squeeze a gas and its pressure rises in exact proportion — the oldest quantitative gas law, and the reason a syringe works.
equations.Name: Boyle's Law

equations.Symbols: a scale factor of the universe · ȧ, ä its first and second time derivatives · H = ȧ/a Hubble parameter · G gravitational constant · ρ density · p pressure · k spatial curvature (−1, 0, +1) · Λ cosmological constant · c speed of light
equations.Significance: Whether the expansion speeds up or slows down. Matter and pressure put on the brakes; the cosmological constant steps on the gas — exactly what the 1998 supernova surveys found the universe doing.
equations.Name: Second Friedmann Equation

equations.Symbols: a scale factor of the universe · ȧ, ä its first and second time derivatives · H = ȧ/a Hubble parameter · G gravitational constant · ρ density · p pressure · k spatial curvature (−1, 0, +1) · Λ cosmological constant · c speed of light
equations.Significance: How fast the universe expands, given what it contains — Einstein's field equations applied to a uniform cosmos. The Hubble parameter, the critical density, and the fate of the universe all fall out of this one line.
equations.Name: First Friedmann Equation

equations.Symbols: e Euler's number · i imaginary unit · π ratio of circumference to diameter
equations.Significance: Five fundamental constants in one exact statement — routinely voted the most beautiful equation in mathematics.
equations.Name: Euler's Identity

equations.Symbols: E electric field · ρ charge density · ε₀ permittivity of free space
equations.Significance: Electric charge is the source of the electric field. One quarter of Maxwell's equations, and the reason field lines start and end on charges.
equations.Name: Gauss's Law

equations.Symbols: E photon energy · h Planck constant · ν frequency of light
equations.Significance: Light comes in packets whose energy scales with frequency — the crack in classical physics that opened into quantum theory.
equations.Name: Planck–Einstein Relation

equations.Symbols: S entropy · k Boltzmann constant · W number of microscopic arrangements
equations.Significance: Entropy counts the ways. The bridge between the microscopic world of atoms and the macroscopic arrow of time — carved on Boltzmann's gravestone.
equations.Name: Boltzmann Entropy

equations.Symbols: p pressure · V volume · n amount of gas (moles) · R gas constant · T absolute temperature
equations.Significance: The behaviour of dilute gases in one line — weather balloons, engine cylinders, and lung volumes to first approximation.
equations.Name: Ideal Gas Law

equations.Symbols: G_μν spacetime curvature · Λ cosmological constant · g_μν metric · T_μν energy and momentum content
equations.Significance: Matter tells spacetime how to curve; curved spacetime tells matter how to move. Black holes, gravitational waves, and the expanding universe live here.
equations.Name: Einstein Field Equations

equations.Symbols: ψ wavefunction · ℏ reduced Planck constant · Ĥ Hamiltonian (total energy) operator · i imaginary unit
equations.Significance: How quantum states evolve in time. Everything from chemistry's periodic trends to semiconductors falls out of solving it.
equations.Name: Schrödinger Equation

equations.Symbols: F gravitational force · G gravitational constant · m₁, m₂ the two masses · r distance between them
equations.Significance: The same rule pulls an apple to the ground and holds the Moon in orbit — the first law to unify heaven and Earth.
equations.Name: Law of Universal Gravitation

equations.Symbols: F net force · m mass · a acceleration
equations.Significance: The workhorse of classical mechanics: push something, and its motion changes in proportion. Rockets, bridges, and billiards all answer to it.
equations.Name: Newton's Second Law

equations.Symbols: E energy · m rest mass · c speed of light in vacuum
equations.Significance: A little mass is worth an enormous amount of energy — the bookkeeping behind nuclear power, stellar fusion, and particle physics.
equations.Name: Mass–energy equivalence
